stories.title: Gauge tests documentation changes against recorded coding-agent sessions
stories.summary: Gauge opens its command-line tool for testing how coding agents use documentation, then comparing proposed fixes against the same tasks.
body: Gauge is a command-line tool for measuring how coding agents use a software product. Its developer announced an open-source release that runs tasks, records session transcripts and tests changes to documentation or other agent-facing material. The problem is practical: an agent may misunderstand a product limitation or repeat a workaround because of the pages it reads.

First, a team defines tasks that require the documentation and runs agents against them. Reviewers then examine the transcripts for friction or failures. Next, they create documentation variants and rerun the tasks with those variants substituted at the same hostname. The developer recommends paired experiments that change only the content and measure the resulting behavior.

The local backend uses Docker containers and a separate network gateway based on mitmproxy for each session. The gateway substitutes documentation and replaces credentials with placeholders. Local execution needs no Gauge account, although model inference remains remote. The announcement describes internal examples of correcting agent misconceptions; those reports are developer claims, rather than independent evidence that the loop improves every product.
stories.takeaway: For developer-tool teams: use repeatable tasks and transcript evidence to check whether a documentation fix changes agent behavior.

stories.title: Langfuse describes an evidence-first path from agent tests to production
stories.summary: The guide starts with offline traces, expert-reviewed examples and repeatable evaluations before extending monitoring to live traffic.
body: Langfuse is an observability and evaluation platform for AI applications. Its new guide describes how regulated teams can collect evidence before allowing an agent to act in production. It addresses the tension between reviewing every answer manually and letting an insufficiently tested system handle consequential work.

The proposed workflow begins with tracing: record prompts, models, tool calls, retrieved context and human approvals, while masking sensitive fields before storage. Teams then run synthetic, historical or shadow examples. Domain experts inspect the resulting traces, identify the first failure and group recurring problems into categories. Those failures and the organization’s requirements become evaluation criteria, using code checks where possible and model judges when judgment is needed.

Experts next build expected outcomes and resolve disagreements in their labels. Teams compare experiments against a baseline and may reserve a held-out dataset to check overfitting. After launch, selected evaluations and user feedback monitor live behavior; interesting traces become new test cases. The guide recommends reducing human review only as evidence supports it. This is a vendor-authored workflow, not a guarantee of regulatory compliance or measured deployment success.
stories.takeaway: For teams introducing agents into reviewed workflows: agree on failure criteria and expected outcomes before expanding autonomous handling.

stories.title: BotGauge links adversarial agent tests to traces and release evaluations
stories.publisher: BotGauge · company announcement via ACCESS Newswire
stories.summary: The company’s launch connects simulated attacks, execution records and repeatable evaluations in one workflow.
body: BotGauge AI is an agent testing and monitoring platform that brings red teaming, tracing and evaluations together. Its launch announcement describes a feedback loop for failures that can appear when a model, prompt or tool changes. Red teaming means deliberately probing a system with adversarial scenarios rather than checking only expected requests.

First, teams run attack scenarios against an agent. BotGauge says the platform includes more than 200 strategies covering prompt injection, policy bypass, tool misuse and manipulation across multiple conversation turns, with support for custom business scenarios. When a test exposes a failure, the tracing layer records the prompts, responses, context, tool calls and execution path behind it.

The finding then becomes an evaluation for subsequent releases. Model-based evaluators assess goal completion, accuracy and adherence to policy so teams can track behavior as their system changes. The company says a lightweight software development kit connects existing model providers and agent frameworks. These are launch claims: the announcement provides no independent comparison of attack coverage, detection accuracy or the ability to prevent recurring failures.
stories.takeaway: For agent-testing teams: check whether a discovered failure can be replayed with its original execution evidence before relying on a regression score.

stories.title: Phoenix preserves failed-task status in experiment traces
stories.summary: A client patch retains error status on failed experiment tasks and preserves instructions during prompt conversion.
body: Phoenix is an AI observability and evaluation platform whose client records experiment tasks as trace spans, records of individual operations. A client patch fixes those records so failed tasks retain their error status. The same patch preserves system and developer instructions when converting prompts to Anthropic, while omitting empty text blocks from the system array. These are narrow correctness fixes: the release note does not describe a broader evaluation redesign or quantify the impact on earlier experiments.
stories.brief_reason: The primary client release contains only two short correctness notes; a full-length story would require unsupported implementation detail.
stories.takeaway: For Phoenix experiment users: verify a deliberately failing task remains marked as failed, and inspect converted instructions when comparing model behavior.

stories.title: Langfuse’s gateway beta links model spending to individual keys
stories.summary: The gateway forwards native model requests and records usage, with separate capture modes for full content or usage alone.
body: Langfuse is an AI observability platform that records model calls and their costs. Its AI Gateway public beta adds a forwarding service for OpenAI and Anthropic requests, aimed at teams that want individual access keys and spending visibility without sharing provider credentials or adding tracing code.

An administrator first stores provider credentials, enables allowed models and chooses the project that receives traces. Teammates then create gateway keys and change their client’s base URL and key. The gateway preserves the native request format, including streaming, rather than translating between provider APIs. User keys stop working when their owner loses access; service account keys support shared workloads.

On Langfuse Cloud, each request becomes a recorded generation. Organizations choose full input and output capture or usage-only capture without prompts and responses. Analytics separates cost, requests and tokens by user, key and model, while gateway-role members see their own usage. Missing model prices produce an alert. Provider processing still follows the customer’s provider agreement, and recorded generations are billable observations. During beta, routes, headers and behavior may change.
stories.takeaway: For teams sharing model access: test key attribution, capture settings and missing-price handling before treating gateway totals as complete spending evidence.

stories.title: OpenInference keeps output and token counts when model streams fail
stories.summary: The JavaScript OpenAI integration records terminal incomplete and failed Responses events, preserving evidence previously missing from those spans.
body: OpenInference provides instrumentation that records AI model activity in traces. Its JavaScript OpenAI integration now retains output and token counts from Responses streams that end incomplete or failed. A span is the trace record for one operation; previously, these streams left an error-marked span without the output or usage that could explain what happened.

The change expands which final stream events the integration keeps. It previously retained only the completed event. It now also records the response carried by incomplete and failed events, so their output and token information remain available. The release gives reaching the output-token limit as an example of an incomplete response.

Status handling still distinguishes the two cases. A failed response remains an error, while an incomplete response is recorded like a completed one. Consequently, the presence of recorded output does not mean a model finished its requested work. The release documents a telemetry correction, without claiming that it prevents model failures or changes the provider’s response.
stories.takeaway: For teams reviewing streaming costs or failures: test incomplete and failed responses separately, and check response state alongside span status.

research.note: Scoped primary-source sweep, not exhaustive web coverage. All 22 existing issues and 127 stories loaded, with primary URLs, event keys, headlines and potentially overlapping content checked. Supplied discovery preserved: fetch:sources would overwrite a path outside authorized run writes, so equivalent read-only HN queries and eight GitHub watchlist checks were performed and logged under this run. All query pages fit a single response; official HN API items verified. All 11 configured News surfaces returned HTTP 200. Splunk listing is a limited shell, supplemented by exact-date search; Datadog searches found events and financial results rather than an eligible original technical story. Transient web failures for Elastic, AskHandle, ACCESS Newswire and HN recovered via direct HTTP/API; Langfuse changelog succeeded in web tool after a direct SSL error. No failed critical source remains. Glow dates excluded rather than using HN submission time. Langfuse gateway beta is a distinct launch/workflow announcement from earlier incremental gateway changes. Original PNGs preserved; one oversized WebP conversion attempt required simpler built-in regeneration, not an alternate image service.

editorial_review.notes: Each story introduces its own product, states the supported problem and mechanism, and retains evidence limits. No dates or versions in narrative. Phoenix brief stays within its two release notes. Source tabs remain separate classifications; evaluation stories grouped. No regulatory guidance claims or guaranteed outcomes.
